summary: The IAB's comments on architecture and policy for Open Pluggable Edge Services (OPES), which are application-level services like a web proxy transforming content between server and client. It discusses concerns such as consent and visibility. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Some helpers in the middle change web pages on their way to you. These architects explain what to worry about so such helpers are honest and visible.

questions: what is one party consent in opes
subtitle: The IAB's checklist of integrity, consent and privacy issues that any in-network content-editing service must address.

tldr.problem: Open Pluggable Edge Services (OPES) would let application-level intermediaries such as web proxy caches transform content, which raises worries about the end-to-end integrity and privacy of data.
tldr.mechanism: The IAB sets out considerations that any OPES framework must address: one-party consent, explicit IP-layer addressing, notification, non-blocking access to the original, URI resolution, reference validity and privacy.
tldr.outcome: The memo recommends what the IESG should require of OPES documents. It does not specify a protocol or advise whether to charter OPES.

today: RFC 3238 is an Informational IAB memo, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It makes recommendations and defines no protocol.

sections.title: What OPES Are and Why the IAB Wrote This
sections.content:
Open Pluggable Edge Services (OPES) are services deployed at application-level intermediaries, for example at a web proxy cache between the origin server and the client, that transform or filter content. Proposed examples include assembling personalized web pages, adding regional information, virus scanning, content adaptation for limited bandwidth and language translation.

The IAB writes about architectural and policy issues raised while chartering OPES in the IETF. The document does not recommend specific solutions, mandate functional requirements or advise the IESG whether to charter OPES. Instead it lists issues that any OPES solution should address, much like the Security Considerations section. The IAB expects that some OPES service will eventually misbehave and some intermediary will be compromised, so the architecture should help end hosts detect and respond to inappropriate behavior.
sections.plainLanguage: Some helpers sit between you and a website and change the page, for example by translating it. The architects wrote down what must be true so these helpers cannot cheat without anyone noticing.

sections.title: The Chartering Controversy and Consent
sections.content:
The RFC quotes a range of opinions, from a view that OPES is deeply evil to a concern that it would reduce the integrity of communications and increase uncertainty about what happened to content in transit. One issue is the one-party consent model, where only one end (the content provider or the end user) must authorize the service. A cited critique says relying on it alone could facilitate third-party or state-sponsored censorship without the knowledge of end users.

The IAB agrees that one-party consent must be required, but agrees that it is insufficient on its own to protect data integrity. It also accepts that implementations could probably be modified to evade any mechanism, as with transport or routing protocols, and argues this is a reason to design infrastructure to detect and defend against compromised implementations, not a reason to avoid standardizing. Digital signatures are a first step, but extra protection is desirable. If OPES is chartered, the working group must also decide whether the architecture is compatible with end-to-end encryption.

The architectural benefit is real: a service at a regional cache can avoid fetching more data from the provider and avoid delay. The costs should be weighed as RFC 3135 did for performance-enhancing proxies (RFC 3135).
sections.plainLanguage: People argued about whether helpers in the middle are a good idea. The architects say they can be useful, but at least one side must say yes to a helper, and that alone is not enough to keep things honest.

sections.title: End-to-End Integrity
sections.content:
The RFC separates three kinds of service: client-centric services acting on responses (virus scanning, translation), server-centric services (a content provider inserting regional news or weather), and client-centric services acting on requests (removing HTTP header fields for privacy, filtering by URL).

For client-centric services on responses, the user has little control over a network virus scanner compared with one on their own machine. The RFC walks through a scanner that rejects a paper about viruses, either by mistake or because it was hacked. Content providers are likely to have the strongest incentive to notice such problems, so the framework should let them be notified and tell users. For server-centric services, the end user needs notification that OPES services were applied and a way to get the non-OPES version, if one exists. For services on requests, the requirements will probably have to be decided case by case.

Considerations 3.1 and 3.2 call for notification to content providers and to end users. Consideration 3.3 says the architecture must not prevent users from retrieving a non-OPES version from the content provider.
sections.plainLanguage: If a helper wrongly blocks or changes a page, both the website owner and you should be able to find out. And you should always be able to ask the website directly for the untouched page.

sections.title: Application Layer Addresses
sections.content:
URIs normally give the same result no matter where the client resolves them, though in practice ad strippers and load-balancing farms already differ. The RFC says URI resolution standards apply unchanged between the client and the OPES intermediary, and the intermediary is the endpoint of resolution. In client-centric OPES, the intermediary resolves the URI for the client. In server-centric OPES, the origin server cedes authority over appropriate content to the intermediary.

Two concerns follow. Changed content may break inter- and intra-document references over a series of interactions. And content might become reachable only through an intermediary, with no non-OPES version, which should not be allowed or would call for an extension to the application addressing architecture.
sections.plainLanguage: A web address should lead to the real page. If a helper edits the page, links inside it must still work, and the page must not exist only through the helper.

sections.title: Privacy
sections.content:
Intermediaries in the middle of the network add places where the privacy of an end-to-end transaction could be compromised. Some of the concern applies to web caches and content distribution networks in general. For OPES to be chartered, the IAB considers it reasonable to require mechanisms for end users to determine the privacy policies of OPES intermediaries, which may differ between client-centric and server-centric services.

The requirement that the overall architecture address privacy does not mean the IETF or the OPES working group must develop every mechanism. The RFC's formal security section adds that the document proposes no new protocols and so involves no security considerations in that sense, and it has no IANA considerations.
sections.plainLanguage: Each extra helper is another place where someone could peek at what you are doing. So you should be able to learn the helper's privacy rules.

sections.title: Summary of IAB Considerations
sections.content:
Section 6 gathers all the considerations in one list. They are the actual output of the memo: consent from at least one end, explicit addressing at the IP layer, notification, non-blocking access to the original content, clarity that services apply to the result of URI resolution, reference validity, no ad hoc addressing fixes and privacy-policy discovery.

Consideration 2.2 does not forbid a chain of intermediaries, as long as the first one is explicitly addressed at the IP layer by the end user.
sections.plainLanguage: The architects boil it down to a short list of rules that every in-the-middle helper must follow to be trusted.

items.label: One-party consent
items.desc: Any OPES service must be explicitly authorized by the content provider or the client.

items.label: IP-layer communications
items.desc: The OPES intermediary must be explicitly addressed at the IP layer by the end user.

items.label: Notification (providers)
items.desc: Help content providers detect and respond to inappropriate client-centric actions.

items.label: Notification (users)
items.desc: Help end users detect the behavior of OPES intermediaries.

items.label: Non-blocking
items.desc: Do not prevent users from retrieving a non-OPES version from the content provider.

items.label: URI resolution
items.desc: Describe services as applied to the result of URI resolution, not as resolution itself.

items.label: Reference validity
items.desc: Each service must define its impact on inter- and intra-document references.

items.label: No ad hoc fixes
items.desc: Services needing more may be reviewed as addressing architecture extensions.

items.label: Privacy
items.desc: Provide mechanisms for end users to determine intermediaries' privacy policies.
